title: A Giant Rodent Lived in Thailand Long Ago
summary:
Imagine a rodent the size of a dog, running through a forest 34 million years ago. Two fossil teeth from a Thai mine belonged to a new species called Yakamys sirindhornae.

The fossils were found at the Bang Mark Pit in the Krabi lignite mine. Scientists from McGill University, Thailand's Department of Mineral Resources, and French research groups studied them. All that was left was two teeth: a lower second molar and a lower incisor.

To guess its size, the team used seven ways to work out weight from tooth size. Their best guess is about 30 kilograms, about 66 pounds — twice as heavy as other rodents of the time, including one called Hulgana.

But the guess is far from sure. Virginie Millien of McGill University called it 'only a ballpark figure.'

The name Yakamys joins 'yak,' the Thai word for giant, with 'mys,' the Greek word for mouse or rat. It honors Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn. Until now, giant rodents were thought to have grown up mostly in South America, but this find points to Southeast Asia.
why_it_matters: Learning how scientists guess an animal's size from just two teeth shows you how to solve a big puzzle from tiny clues, just like you do in school.

keywords.explanation: A rodent is an animal with big front teeth for gnawing, like a mouse or a rat.
A molar is one of the big flat teeth at the back of the mouth that you use for chewing.
An incisor is a sharp front tooth used for biting and cutting food.
Lignite is a soft brown coal that forms from old plants buried in the ground.
Yakamys sirindhornae is the name scientists gave to this giant rodent that lived long ago.

background_read: A fossil is what is left of a living thing from long ago, like a tooth or a bone that turned to stone in the ground.
Scientists study fossils to learn what animals looked like and how they lived.
Even a single tooth can give clues about an animal's size, because bigger animals often have bigger teeth.
